passages.title: The Red Planet: Mars
paragraphs: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. When you look at it through a telescope, it looks orange-red. That is why people call it the Red Planet.
Mars gets its color from its dusty ground. The dust has iron in it, and the iron has turned to rust, just like an old bike left out in the rain.
The planet was named after Mars, the Roman god of war. The Romans thought its red color looked like the color of battle.

Mars has two small moons called Phobos and Deimos. It also has the tallest volcano we know of in the whole solar system. It is called Olympus Mons, and it is about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest!
No people have visited Mars yet, but robot rovers are exploring it. They take pictures and study rocks to learn if tiny living things were ever there.

passages.title: Busy Honeybees
paragraphs: A honeybee may be tiny, but it is a very hard worker. Honeybees live together in a big group called a colony. A colony can have thousands of bees!
Every colony has one queen bee. Her job is to lay eggs. Most of the other bees are worker bees. They build the hive, keep it clean, look after the baby bees and gather food.
Worker bees fly from flower to flower to drink a sweet liquid called nectar. Back at the hive, they turn the nectar into honey and store it in little wax rooms called cells.
How does a bee tell its friends where the best flowers are? It dances! Its wiggly waggle dance shows the other bees which way to fly and how far to go.
Bees also carry pollen from one flower to another. This helps plants make seeds and fruit. Without bees, we would have much less food to eat.

options: Bees carry pollen that helps plants make seeds and fruit

passages.title: The Ugly Duckling
paragraphs: One summer, a mother duck sat on her nest by the pond. One by one, her eggs cracked open and fluffy yellow ducklings came out. But the last egg was the biggest, and the bird that hatched from it was large and gray.
"What an ugly duckling!" the other animals said. They teased him and pushed him away. The little bird felt so sad and lonely that he ran away from the farm.
All through the cold winter, he hid among the tall reeds of a frozen lake. He was cold and hungry, but he did not give up.
When spring came, he saw beautiful white birds gliding on the water. He swam to them shyly. Then he looked down at his reflection. He was not a gray duckling anymore. He was a graceful white swan!
The other swans welcomed him, and he was happy at last.

What lesson does the story teach?
options: Be kind, because everyone grows in their own way

passages.title: Elephants: The Largest Land Animals
paragraphs: Elephants are the largest animals that live on land. An adult African elephant can weigh as much as a small truck!
An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together, and it is very useful. Elephants use their trunks to breathe, smell, drink water, pick up food and even greet each other.
Elephants live in family groups called herds. The oldest and wisest female, called the matriarch, leads the herd. She remembers where to find food and water, even in dry seasons.
Elephants also have big ears. On hot days, they flap their ears like fans to help cool their bodies down.

passages.title: The Sun: Our Nearest Star
paragraphs: Every morning, the Sun rises and lights up our day. But did you know the Sun is a star? It is the star closest to Earth.
The Sun is a giant ball of very hot, glowing gas. It is so big that more than a million Earths could fit inside it!
The Sun is about 150 million kilometers away from us. Its light travels so fast that it reaches Earth in about eight minutes.
Plants need sunlight to grow, and the Sun keeps our planet warm. Without the Sun, there would be no life on Earth.
Remember: never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses on. Its strong light can hurt your eyes.

passages.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
paragraphs: A young shepherd boy watched over his village's sheep on a hill. The days were long, and he was bored.
One day, he shouted, "Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is chasing the sheep!" The villagers ran up the hill to help, but there was no wolf. The boy laughed at them.
A few days later, he did it again. Once more, the villagers came running, and once more, there was no wolf. This time they were very angry.
Then, one evening, a real wolf came. "Wolf! Wolf!" the boy cried. But no one came, because no one believed him anymore. The wolf scattered the sheep.
Nobody believes a liar, even when he is telling the truth.

options: He was bored and wanted to trick the villagers

options: The villagers came running again, but there was no wolf

questions.prompt: Why did no one come when the real wolf appeared?
questions.answerText: They did not believe him anymore

questions.prompt: What is the lesson of the story?
options: If you tell lies, people may not believe you when you tell the truth
